cards.front: Recall a key point about Perception
cards.back: Perception is the process of interpreting sensory information to make sense of the world. Sensation is detecting stimuli; perception is interpreting them - they are distinct processes.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Perception
cards.back: Gregory's constructivist theory: perception uses past experience and expectations to interpret sensory input (top-down processing). Visual illusions support this - we misinterpret because we apply assumptions (e.g. the Muller-Lyer illusion).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Perception
cards.back: Gibson's direct theory: perception is entirely determined by sensory input from the environment (bottom-up processing). We perceive affordances - what the environment offers us (e.g. a chair affords sitting). No past experience needed.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Perception
cards.back: Factors affecting perception: culture (Hudson's study showed Western and non-Western people perceive depth cues differently), emotion (anxious people perceive threats more readily), motivation (hungry people are more likely to perceive food-related images).

cards.front: Recall a key point about Perception
cards.back: Visual illusions reveal how perception can be distorted: the Ames Room exploits size constancy; the Kanizsa Triangle shows we perceive shapes that don't physically exist (illusory contours).

cards.front: What should you know about psychology exam tips?
cards.back: When evaluating perception theories, consider whether perception is more influenced by nature (Gibson - innate) or nurture (Gregory - learned). Support your argument with specific studies and acknowledge that both processes likely contribute.

Students often make mistakes here. Wrong: Perception is entirely determined by the information available in the environment, so visual illusions cannot exist. Correct: Visual illusions clearly demonstrate that perception is not simply a direct read-out of environmental information - the brain must be interpreting sensory input using assumptions and expectations. cards.front: Key Studies and Theories in Perception
cards.back: Perception is a core topic in GCSE Psychology that requires understanding of key studies, theories and research methods. The AQA, OCR and Edexcel specifications all require you to know specific studies in detail, evaluate their methodology, and apply psychological concepts to real-life scenarios.
